title: Background-free and laser-ionization minimized single-shot fs-EFISH in luminous pulsed plasmas
summary: This work introduces spectrally tuned electric field induced second harmonic (t-EFISH) generation for substantially reducing or eliminating background plasma emission in single-shot, time-resolved, electric field measurements. The technique is demonstrated using a femtosecond 1240 nm pump and 620 nm signal detection to avoid spectral and temporal overlap with the early, intense onset of N2(C-B) emission in nanosecond atmospheric-pressure air spark discharges. This enhances signal-to-emission ratios pre- and post-breakdown, enables lower pump energies, suppresses detector saturation, and reduces the coefficient of variation in the electric field measurements by 8.5x. This strategy also provides a pathway for background-free measurements in other discharge environments with varying spectro-temporal emission characteristics. Moreover, the longer 1240 nm pump wavelength reduces multiphoton intrusiveness, directly improving measurement fidelity.

title: High-power X-Point Target divertor experiments on the TCV tokamak
summary: Stationary power exhaust in the X-Point Target (XPT) divertor configuration is investigated in high-power ($2.5\,\text{MW}$) TCV L-mode discharges, in which the Lengyel detachment scaling metric $P_{\text{SOL}}B_{0}/(R_{0}n_{e,\text{u}}^{2})$ lies in the range expected for reactors (SPARC, ITER, ARC). Compared with a conventional single-null (SN) divertor, the XPT improves power exhaust performance, reducing the peak outer target heat flux by 40--60\% and enabling divertor detachment with nitrogen seeding under conditions in which the SN cannot be detached. Detachment evolves asymmetrically across the multiple XPT outer strike points. The sensitivities of the peak target heat fluxes and impurity emission front positions to the X-point separation ($\text{d}R_{\text{u},X2}$) are characterized and found to decrease at higher nitrogen seeding levels. Field-reversal experiments reveal the critical role of $E\times B$ drifts inherent to the magnetic topology of the secondary X-point, which drive an unconventional redistribution of density and impurity radiation in the XPT divertor and thereby cause the asymmetries between the XPT outer strike points, largely confirming the expectations from recent SOLPS-ITER modelling. A framework for understanding the power exhaust physics of the XPT is presented, detailing the roles of SOL splitting, connection length peaking, $E\times B$ drifts, and vessel geometry. Together, these results establish an experimental physics basis for the XPT divertor as a potential power exhaust solution for tokamak reactors.

title: Drive and damping govern resonant electron energy redistribution in a kinetic model informed by helium discharges
summary: Energetic electrons exchange energy with electrostatic waves in low-temperature plasmas, but wave amplitude alone does not determine the direction or cumulative effect of that exchange. We analyse nonlinear electron redistribution using a single-mode kinetic model parameterized by published helium-discharge measurements. Frequency and pressure comparisons are combined with a controlled damping scan and explicit particle-current and energy diagnostics. Across the frequency cases, the inferred resonant drive varies by a factor of 2.7 while background damping varies by only about 9%. Reducing pressure from 33.3 to 10.66 Pa at 37 MHz increases the net drive by a factor of 2.24. In the damping scan, the peak wave energy and residual parallel-energy deficit both decrease by approximately 93%, consistent with quadratic field-amplitude scaling at the reported endpoints. An integrated energy identity connects retained wave energy, background loss and distribution recovery, and distinguishes cessation of wave growth from reversal of energy transfer. Quantitative timescale and directional-distribution tests define the connection between this reduced model and discharge kinetics. The analysis provides a common interpretation of resonant redistribution, coherent current and energy exchange, together with observables for testing that interpretation in kinetic simulations and phase-resolved measurements.

title: Analytic Solution to Cumulative Coulomb Scattering in Boltzmann Theory
summary: In plasmas, frequent soft Coulomb collisions gradually transfer energy and momentum, whereas a single close collision can change both abruptly and redirect a particle. This coexistence can shape runaway-electron avalanches in tokamaks and alpha-particle heating in inertial fusion, yet no first-principles analytic theory has determined how the cumulative statistics evolve under plasma conditions. Fokker--Planck and moment-matched models reproduce average transport but do not determine how scattering evolves from isolated events to cumulative relaxation across plasma conditions. Here we resolve this long-standing problem directly from Boltzmann theory. By asymptotically rescaling the exact angular expansion, we obtain the first quantitative map of the single-collision, core-tail coexistence, and low-order relaxation regimes within a unified Boltzmann framework. The rescaling also provides explicit analytic representations of the angular distribution across these regimes without empirical transition parameters. The theory further shows that small-angle models differ from the Boltzmann distribution even in the forward core, so appending a large-angle tail to a conventional core cannot recover the collision statistics. In fast-electron transport, this full-range redistribution leaves mean energy loss nearly unchanged yet counterintuitively enhances beam concentration and modifies the energy flux delivered to a finite region.

title: Compact plasma-based extreme compression of relativistic electron beams
summary: Accelerated particle beams are essential tools of modern science and technology with applications ranging from medicine [1], to light sources [2], to high-energy physics [3]. Over time, as accelerator-based experiments become more sophisticated and probe natural phenomena with greater temporal resolution, there is an increasing demand on beam parameters, in particular on bunch duration. Experiments have been proposed that require beams with 1-2 orders of magnitude shorter durations than what is possible with current state-of-the-art technology. However, state-of-the-art temporal bunch compressors force a trade-off between how short an electron bunch can be made and how well its transverse quality survives the strong bending magnets required to do so -- a limitation that stands as a grand challenge for accelerator physics to-date [4]. In this experiment, we demonstrate a new, compact compression technique for generating ultrashort, high-peak-current electron bunches that circumvents this trade-off using plasma wakefield acceleration. Just as chirped pulse amplification unlocked ultrashort, high-power laser pulses and the technologies that followed from them, here we demonstrate an analogous chirp-and-compress strategy applied to relativistic electron beams by using the extreme electric fields of a plasma wakefield in place of a stretcher-amplifier, thereby unlocking the path to ultrashort, extremely high-current electron beams. We demonstrate the first application of this plasma-compressed bunch using it to drive single-microbunch free electron lasing at optical wavelengths in a single, meter-scale undulator module, producing radiation pulses roughly four orders of magnitude more energetic than the first beam-driven, plasma-based free electron laser demonstration at the same accelerator facility [5, 6].

title: Filamentary dynamics in fan-like structures in high-altitude lightning discharges
summary: We present LOFAR radio telescope measurements revealing that high-altitude negative leaders (HANLs) exhibit behavior completely different from the current paradigm of negative leader propagation. Our data show that the fan at the tip of a propagating HANL is formed by filaments that behave like smoothly advancing negative leaders. These negative leader filaments appear to have moderate conductivity, remain thin (radius $\sim1$ m), grow continuously at $\sim10^5$ m/s over hundreds of meters, and emit VHF radiation persistently. The observations show that the filaments making up the fan in front of a propagating negative leader are not necessarily streamers, as commonly assumed. Previous work suggesting to observe streamers at the tips of negative leaders should be re-examined in light of these new findings
